L9: # Title:The Curse of Recursion: Training on Generated Data Makes Models Forget
L10: 
L11: Authors:cite6†Ilia Shumailov , cite7†Zakhar Shumaylov , cite8†Yiren Zhao , cite9†Yarin Gal , cite10†Nicolas Papernot , cite11†Ross Anderson L12:

L15: cite12†View PDF cite13†HTML (experimental) L16: > Abstract:Stable Diffusion revolutionised image creation from descriptive text. GPT-2, GPT-3(.5) and GPT-4 demonstrated astonishing performance across a variety of language tasks. ChatGPT introduced such language models to the general public. It is now clear that large language models (LLMs) are here to stay, and will bring about drastic change in the whole ecosystem of online text and images. In this paper we consider what the future might hold.
L17: What will happen to GPT-{n} once LLMs contribute much of the language found online? We find that use of model-generated content in training causes irreversible defects in the resulting models, where tails of the original content distribution disappear. We refer to this effect as Model Collapse and show that it can occur in Variational Autoencoders, Gaussian Mixture Models and LLMs. We build theoretical intuition behind the phenomenon and portray its ubiquity amongst all learned generative models.
L18: We demonstrate that it has to be taken seriously if we are to sustain the benefits of training from large-scale data scraped from the web. Indeed, the value of data collected about genuine human interactions with systems will be increasingly valuable in the presence of content generated by LLMs in data crawled from the Internet.

L0@P0: Self-Distillation Amplifies Regularization
L1@P0: in Hilbert Space
L2@P0: Hossein Mobahi♣ Mehrdad Farajtabar§ Peter L. Bartlett♣‡
L3@P0: hmobahi@google.com farajtabar@google.com bartlett@eecs.berkeley.edu
L4@P0: ♣ Google Research, Mountain View, CA, USA
L5@P0: § DeepMind, Mountain View, CA, USA
L6@P0: ‡ EECS Dept., University of California at Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA
L7@P0: Abstract
L8@P0: Knowledge distillation introduced in the deep learning context is a method to
L9@P0: transfer knowledge from one architecture to another. In particular, when the
L10@P0: architectures are identical, this is called self-distillation. The idea is to feed in
L11@P0: predictions of the trained model as new target values for retraining (and iterate
L12@P0: this loop possibly a few times). It has been empirically observed that the selfdistilled model often achieves higher accuracy on held out data. Why this happens,
L13@P0: however, has been a mystery: the self-distillation dynamics does not receive any
L14@P0: new information about the task and solely evolves by looping over training. To
L15@P0: the best of our knowledge, there is no rigorous understanding of why this happens.
L16@P0: This work provides the first theoretical analysis of self-distillation. We focus on
L17@P0: fitting a nonlinear function to training data, where the model space is Hilbert space
L18@P0: and fitting is subject to �2 regularization in this function space. We show that selfdistillation iterations modify regularization by progressively limiting the number
L19@P0: of basis functions that can be used to represent the solution. This implies (as we
L20@P0: also verify empirically) that while a few rounds of self-distillation may reduce
L21@P0: over-fitting, further rounds may lead to under-fitting and thus worse performance.
L22@P0: 1 Introduction
L23@P0: Knowledge Distillation. Knowledge distillation was introduced in the deep learning setting [13]
L24@P0: as a method for transferring knowledge from one architecture (teacher) to another (student), with
L25@P0: the student model often being smaller (see also [5] for earlier ideas). This is achieved by training
L26@P0: the student model using the output probability distribution of the teacher model in addition to
L27@P0: original labels. The student model benefits from this “dark knowledge” (extra information in soft
L28@P0: predictions) and often performs better than if it was trained on the actual labels. Various extensions
L29@P0: of this approach have been recently proposed, where instead of output predictions, the student
L30@P0: tries to match other statistics from the teacher model such as intermediate feature representations
L31@P0: [27], Jacobian matrices [31], distributions [15], Gram matrices [37]. Additional developments on
L32@P0: knowledge distillation include its extensions to Bayesian settings [17, 34], uncertainty preservation
L33@P0: [33], reinforcement learning [14, 32, 9], online distillation [19], zero-shot learning [24], multi-step
L34@P0: knowledge distillation [23], tackling catastrophic forgetting [20], transfer of relational knowledge [25],
L35@P0: adversarial distillation [35]. Recently [26] analyzed why the student model is able to mimic teacher
L36@P0: model in knowledge distillation and [21] presented a statistical perspective on distillation.
L37@P0: Self-Distillation. The special case when the teacher and student architectures are identical is called
L38@P0: self-distillation. The idea is to feed in predictions of the trained model as new target values for
L39@P0: retraining (and iterate this loop possibly a few times). It has been consistently observed that the
L40@P0: self-distilled often achieves higher accuracy on held out data [8, 36, 2]. Why this happens, however,
L41@P0: has been a mystery: the self-distillation dynamics does not receive any new information about the
L42@P0-1: 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2020), Vancouver, Canada.task and solely evolves by looping over training. There have been some recent attempts to understand
L43@P1: the mysteries around distillation. [11] have empirically observed that the dark knowledge transferred
L44@P1: by the teacher is localized mainly in higher layers and does not affect early (feature extraction) layers
L45@P1: much. [8] interprets dark knowledge as importance weighting. [6] shows that early-stopping is
L46@P1: crucial for reaching dark-knowledge of self-distillation. [1] empirically studies how inductive biases
L47@P1: are transferred through distillation. Ideas similar to self-distillation have been used in areas besides
L48@P1: modern machine learning but with different names such diffusion and boosting in both the statistics
L49@P1: and image processing communities [22].
L50@P1: Contributions. Despite interesting developments, why distillation can improve generalization
L51@P1: remains elusive. To the best of our knowledge, there is no rigorous understanding of this phenomenon.
L52@P1: This work provides a theoretical analysis of self-distillation. While originally observed in deep
L53@P1: learning, we show that this is a more profound phenomenon that can occur even in classical
L54@P1: regression settings, where we fit a nonlinear function to training data with models belonging to a
L55@P1: Hilbert space and using �2 regularization in this function space. In this setting we show that the
L56@P1: self-distillation iterations progressively limit the number of basis functions used to represent
L57@P1: the solution. This implies (as we also verify empirically) that while a few rounds of self-distillation
L58@P1: may reduce over-fitting, further rounds may lead to under-fitting and thus worse performance.
L59@P1: More precisely, we show that self-distillation results in a non-conventional power iteration where
L60@P1: the linear operation changes dynamically; each step depends intricately on the results of earlier
L61@P1: linear operations via a nonlinear recurrence. We also prove that using lower training error across
L62@P1: distillation steps generally improves the sparsity effect, and specifically we provide a closed
L63@P1: form bound on the sparsity level as the training error goes to zero. Finally, we discuss how our
L64@P1: regularization results can be translated into generalization bounds.
L65@P1: Organization. In Section 2 we setup a variational formulation of nonlinear regression and discuss the
L66@P1: existence of non-trivial solutions. Section 3 formalizes self-distillation in our setting. It then shows
L67@P1: self-distillation iterations at some point collapse the solution. It provides a lower bound on the number
L68@P1: of distillation rounds before the collapse is reached. In addition, it shows that coefficient of the basis
L69@P1: functions initially used to represent the solution gradually progressively become sparser. Finally,
L70@P1: we discuss that by having the models operate in the near-interpolation regime one can ultimately
L71@P1: achieve higher sparsity level. Section 5 draws connection between our setting and the NTK regime of
L72@P1: neural networks. This motivates subsequent experiments on deep neural networks in that section. Full
L73@P1: proofs for these as well as the code for reproducing examples in Sections 4 and results in Section 5
L74@P1: are available in the supplementary appendix.
